item.title: What a full service actually includes
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
"Full service" is not a defined term. It means whatever the garage quoting you decides it means, which is why two quotes for the same words can differ by an hour of labour and four consumable parts.

The list worth asking for

A service that deserves the name replaces the engine oil and its filter, the air filter and the cabin filter, and checks the fluids that are not on a replacement schedule — brake fluid, coolant, screenwash. Spark plugs come out at the interval the manufacturer sets, not every visit.

Beyond the parts, the car should go on a lift so that brakes, suspension joints, exhaust mountings and tyre wear are looked at rather than guessed at from outside.

What you should get back

A written record of what was replaced, what was checked, and what is approaching the end of its life but does not need doing yet. That last category is the one that separates a service report from an invoice.

If a report has no "not yet, but soon" section, either the car is brand new or nobody looked properly.

Keep the paperwork. It is worth real money when you sell the car, and it is what keeps a manufacturer warranty intact when the servicing is done outside the dealer network.
item.excerpt:encoded: Two garages can quote the same price for a "full service" and do very different amounts of work. Here is the list to ask for.

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: Useful list. Mine came back with "brakes checked" and nothing else written down — I will ask for the measurement next time.
Always ask for it in millimetres. Any workshop that measured them can tell you the number without looking twice.

item.title: That warning light, and what it does not mean
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
An engine management light means the car has stored a fault code. The code describes what the car noticed, not what is broken — and the difference between those two things is most of the bill.

An example worth remembering

A code reading "oxygen sensor, bank 1" is frequently not a failed sensor. The sensor is reporting a mixture that is outside the expected range, which a small vacuum leak upstream will do quite happily with a perfectly good sensor fitted.

Replace the sensor and the light goes out for a fortnight. The leak is still there.

What a diagnosis looks like

Read the code, then verify it. Live data while the engine runs, a smoke test if a leak is suspected, and a comparison against what the manufacturer says the reading should be at that temperature and load. Only then is a part worth ordering.

It takes longer on the first visit. It is the reason there is not a second one.
item.excerpt:encoded: A fault code is a symptom with a number on it. Replacing the part the code names is how people end up paying twice.

item.title: Brake pads: when thin becomes urgent
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A new brake pad has somewhere between ten and twelve millimetres of friction material. It is worn out at about three, and most manufacturers want it changed before it reaches two.

Why mileage is a poor guide

The same pads can last eighty thousand miles on a motorway commute and twenty thousand on short urban journeys with a hilly route home. Weight matters, driving style matters more, and towing changes the arithmetic completely.

This is why a garage should tell you the measurement rather than a verdict. "Four millimetres left" tells you roughly a year; "they are getting low" tells you nothing you can plan around.

The noises, in order of urgency

A light squeal on the first application of the morning is usually surface rust and clears in a few stops. A steady metallic scrape is the wear indicator or the backing plate, and that one is not a next-month job.

A pulsing pedal is a separate problem: that is the disc, not the pad.
item.excerpt:encoded: Pads wear at very different rates depending on how and where you drive. Millimetres, not months, are what matter.

item.title: Getting the air conditioning ready before summer
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
An air conditioning system is not sealed the way a fridge is. It loses a small percentage of its refrigerant every year through the flexible hoses and the compressor shaft seal, and that is normal.

Why the timing matters

Everybody discovers their air conditioning is weak in the same fortnight, which is the fortnight it is hardest to get an appointment. Booked in spring it is a routine job.

What a regas should include

Recovering what is left, weighing it, pulling a vacuum to check the system holds it, and refilling to the exact weight the manufacturer specifies. If a system has lost a lot, the honest next step is a leak test with dye rather than simply filling it again.

Refilling a leaking system is not a repair. It is a subscription.

While the system is open, the cabin filter is worth replacing — most of what people describe as a smell from the vents is the filter rather than the system.
item.excerpt:encoded: Systems lose a little refrigerant every year by design. The cheap time to deal with that is before the first warm week.

item.title: Buying a used car: what an inspection finds
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A car that looks straight in a photograph and drives quietly on a ten minute test route can still have several thousand pounds of work waiting for it. Most of what matters is underneath.

What gets found most often

Corrosion on suspension mounting points and sills. Perished bushes that make a car feel vague rather than broken. Evidence of a repair the seller has not mentioned — mismatched paint depth, overspray on a seal, a panel gap that runs out.

Then the ordinary things with a price attached: pads and discs near the end, tyres with uneven wear that points at geometry, a clutch that bites high.

What it is worth

Not because the car is bad. Most are fine. It is worth it because you can either walk away or negotiate with a written list, and a list is a much stronger position than a feeling.
